goals.en:
Upon the successful completion of this course, students will (be able to):

Knowledge:
• Have familiarized themselves with relevant economic theories
• Explain and apply basic microeconomic principles such as demand and supply, competitive market equilibrium and beyond, elasticity and externalities
• Explain and apply basic macroeconomic principles such as economic growth (causes and consequences), international trade and inequality

Skills:
• Interpret data for a fact-based analysis
• Have developed writing, presentation, debating and oral skills
• Have worked in a group setting
• Translate academic knowledge into practical use

description.en:
During this course, students will deal with questions such as: how are prices determined in a competitive market? What role can governments play when markets fail - if any? Are there (moral) limits to markets? How does the presence of monopolies affect an economy? Why are some countries rich while others poor? Why do countries trade? What are the consequences of economic development for inequality and the environment?

In order to answer these questions, the course covers the fundamentals of micro- and macroeconomics. The microeconomics part discusses, among others, economic decision-making by individuals and firms, and the determination of quantities and prices in the market. The macroeconomics part covers topics such as economic growth, trade and inequality. Consequently, the course proposes a unified approach that combines the two fields offering students insights into the interaction between individuals, households, firms and governments, functioning at different levels of the economy.

To different extents, the course addresses the Sustainable Development Goals 1 (no poverty), 3 (well-being), 8 (decent work and economic growth), 9 (innovation), 10 (reduced inequalities), as well as 13 (climate action).

'Principles of Economics' relates to a number of other courses of the GRL program such as the foundation courses 'Explaining Human Behaviour' and 'Politics, Power & International Responsibility'. There are also strong links to the 'Statistics I' course. The theories, methods and applications discussed in this course will form the basis for the following economics courses of the GRL program and, more generally, for the major 'Politics, Philosophy and Economics'.
